analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote, one day after the Medicare drug benefit became law with the price-negotiation ban intact.
analysis.plain_summary: Days after a new Medicare prescription drug benefit became law, this bill would have deleted the clause that forbids the government from using Medicare's huge purchasing power to negotiate drug prices with manufacturers. An HHS inspector general study cited in the bill found Medicare could save nearly a billion dollars a year on medical supplies alone by paying the prices the Veterans Affairs Department negotiates. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would pay less out of pocket for prescriptions, and taxpayers, who fund the Medicare program and would see its drug and supply costs fall if the government could bargain like the VA does.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'noninterference' provision added by the 2003 Medicare drug law, which bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating prices with drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and Medicare drug plan sponsors.

Cites a 2002 HHS inspector general finding that if Medicare paid the same prices for 16 medical supplies that the Department of Veterans Affairs negotiates directly, the federal government would save $958 million a year.
States the findings that barring federal negotiation fails to use Medicare's purchasing power and that negotiating can lower drug costs for both Medicare and taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would face a single large buyer able to bargain prices down, and the private drug plan intermediaries whose role in pricing the benefit would be reduced.

drawbacks.text: Letting the government negotiate directly could reduce the negotiating role of the private drug plans created under the new benefit, raising questions about how the public-private structure of the program would work.

Pharmaceutical makers have long argued that government-negotiated prices would mean less revenue for research on new drugs; the bill text and record do not address how negotiation would be structured or what price targets would apply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a narrow, one-clause fix: it simply struck the ban on negotiation. The potential taxpayer and beneficiary savings, illustrated by the VA comparison, are large, and the main cost would fall on manufacturer revenue rather than on patients. The bill did not spell out the negotiating mechanics, so the design questions were left open — but the bill never got far enough for those questions to be argued.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced December 9, 2003, one day after the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act — which created the new drug benefit and the negotiation ban — was enacted.
Senate Majority Leader... rather, Democratic leader Tom Daschle introduced the bill on Feingold's behalf.
It had no cosponsors and received no committee action, no hearing, and no vote; its last recorded action was the referral to Finance on December 9, 2003.
The prohibition on federal price negotiation it targeted remained in effect throughout the 108th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the negotiation ban that the new Medicare drug law had just given them, and taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries kept paying the prices that private plans negotiate without direct federal bargaining.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the ban on Medicare drug price negotiation; introduced it immediately after the Medicare drug law was signed.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Feingold's behalf on the Senate floor.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, took no action on it; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: Supported keeping the noninterference clause in the new Medicare drug benefit, which bars the government from negotiating prices directly.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held, so there is no roll-call record; the sponsor was a Democrat, no Republican cosponsors joined, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have let the federal government negotiate Part D drug prices directly, eroding manufacturers' pricing power over the largest public buyer of prescriptions. The ban it targeted was enacted in the 2003 Medicare law and remained in place.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Under the 2003 law, private plan sponsors and the intermediaries they hire stand between Medicare and drug prices; direct federal negotiation would have reduced their pricing role. They kept that role because the bill never advanced.

An HHS inspector general study cited in the bill found Medicare overpays for supplies relative to VA-negotiated prices; competition from a negotiating federal buyer could compress those margins, while savings flow to taxpayers.
